==Problem==
A square with integer side length is cut into 10 squares, all of which have integer side length and at least 8 of which have area 1. What is the smallest possible value of the length of the side of the original square?

<math> \text{(A)}\hspace{.05in}3\qquad\text{(B)}\hspace{.05in}4\qquad\text{(C)}\hspace{.05in}5\qquad\text{(D)}\hspace{.05in}6\qquad\text{(E)}\hspace{.05in}7 </math>

==Solution==
The first answer choice <imath> {\textbf{(A)}\ 3} </imath>, can be eliminated since there must be <imath> 10 </imath> squares with integer side lengths. We then test the next smallest side length, which is <imath> 4 </imath>. The square with area <imath> 16 </imath> can be partitioned into <imath> 8 </imath> squares with area <imath> 1 </imath> and two squares with area <imath> 4 </imath>, which satisfies all the conditions of the problem. Therefore, the smallest possible value of the length of the side of the original square is <imath> \boxed{\textbf{(B)}\ 4} </imath>.
